content: The enzyme CYP2C9/10 plays a critical role in drug metabolism. When prescribing medications that are substrates of CYP2C9, therapy should be adjusted, and patients should be closely monitored. Dosage modifications may be necessary based on clinical indications. Non-aspirin salicylates can increase sulfadiazine levels through an unspecified mechanism, but the clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. Similarly, salsalate and transdermal selegiline also elevate sulfadiazine levels via unknown mechanisms, with unclear clinical relevance. Sulfadiazine significantly increases the levels or effects of siponimod by interfering with hepatic CYP2C9/10 metabolism. Co-administration of siponimod with moderate CYP2C9 inhibitors and moderate or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors is not recommended. If siponimod is used with moderate CYP2C9 inhibitors alone, caution is advised, and close monitoring is required. Sulfadiazine reduces the efficacy of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering its metabolism. Antibiotics co-administered with sodium picosulfate can decrease its efficacy by disrupting colonic bacterial flora necessary for drug activation. Close monitoring is recommended. Sparsentan, a CYP2C9 inducer, decreases sulfadiazine levels and reduces the efficacy of CYP2C9 substrates. This interaction necessitates caution and close monitoring. Spironolactone, sulfasalazine, and triamterene increase sulfadiazine levels through unspecified mechanisms, but the clinical significance remains unclear. Sulfadiazine increases terbinafine levels by affecting CYP2C9/10 metabolism, requiring close monitoring. When co-administered with methaemoglobin-inducing drugs, sulfadiazine may increase the risk of methaemoglobinemia, necessitating careful observation for symptoms. Sulfadiazine decreases thiamine levels by altering intestinal flora, but this applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Torsemide and tranylcypromine also increase sulfadiazine levels through unknown mechanisms, with unclear clinical significance. Sulfadiazine and tretinoin (oral or topical) exhibit pharmacodynamic synergism, leading to increased phototoxicity. Alternative drugs should be considered to avoid this serious interaction. Sulfadiazine reduces the efficacy of the live typhoid vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live bacterial vaccines should not be administered until antibiotic therapy is completed. Sulfadiazine and valoctocogene roxaparvovec may both increase the risk of hepatotoxicity. Medications with potential hepatotoxic effects should be closely monitored or replaced with alternatives to minimize liver enzyme elevation. Sulfadiazine and verteporfin exhibit pharmacodynamic synergism, increasing phototoxicity. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. Sulfadiazine and voclosporin may increase each other’s toxicity through nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Co-administration with nephrotoxic drugs increases the risk of acute or chronic kidney damage, necessitating close monitoring. Sulfadiazine increases warfarin levels by inhibiting CYP2C9 and causing protein-binding displacement. If co-administered, the warfarin dose may need to be reduced by 10-20%, and therapy should be closely monitored. Willow bark increases sulfadiazine levels through an unspecified mechanism, but the clinical significance is unknown. Adverse effects of sulfadiazine include diarrhea, headache, reversible oligospermia, anorexia, gastric distress, nausea, photosensitivity, vomiting, allergic reactions (e.g., rash), aplastic anemia, dizziness, hypersensitivity, itching, thyroid dysfunction, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, Lyell’s syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, fever, hemolytic anemia, leukopenia, hepatitis, jaundice, hematuria, acute nephropathy, and interstitial nephritis. Patients with hypersensitivity to the drug or its excipients, infants under two months (except in congenital toxoplasmosis treatment), and pregnant or nursing women should avoid sulfadiazine. Sulfonamides are ineffective against group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infections and do not prevent sequelae like rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis. Fatalities have been reported due to hypersensitivity reactions, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, and other blood dyscrasias. Early signs of serious blood disorders include sore throat, fever, pallor, purpura, or jaundice. Renal complications are less frequent with more soluble sulfonamides. Sulfonamides should be used cautiously in patients with impaired renal or hepatic function, severe allergies, or bronchial asthma. Hemolysis may occur in individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, and this reaction is dose-dependent. Adequate hydration is essential to prevent crystalluria and stone formation. Patients should drink an eight-ounce glass of water with each dose and report symptoms like sore throat, fever, pallor, purpura, or jaundice promptly. The safety of sulfonamides during pregnancy has not been established, and their teratogenic potential remains inadequately studied. Sulfadiazine is contraindicated in nursing mothers due to its ability to cross the placenta, be excreted in breast milk, and cause kernicterus. A decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering its importance to the mother. Sulfadiazine is well-absorbed and distributed into most body tissues, crossing cell membranes freely. Approximately 32-56% of the drug is protein-bound. It is primarily eliminated in the urine, with urinary concentrations 10-25 times higher than serum levels. Sulfadiazine exerts a bacteriostatic effect by competitively antagonizing para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA). Microorganisms requiring exogenous folic acid and unable to synthesize it are not susceptible to sulfonamides. This medication is used to treat and prevent various infections and belongs to the sulfa antibiotic class. It is ineffective against viral infections like the common cold or flu. It should be taken orally with a full glass of water, and adequate fluid intake should be maintained during treatment. The medication should be taken at evenly spaced intervals and completed as prescribed, even if symptoms improve. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite, and headache. Rarely, it may cause severe intestinal conditions due to Clostridium difficile, oral thrush, or vaginal yeast infections. Serious allergic reactions, severe skin rashes (e.g., Stevens-Johnson syndrome), blood disorders, liver damage, or lung injury may occur. Patients should seek medical advice for any concerning symptoms. Before taking sulfadiazine, inform your doctor of any allergies, including to sulfa medications, or other medical conditions. This medication may reduce the efficacy of live bacterial vaccines and increase sun sensitivity. Pregnant women should use this medication only when necessary and avoid it near delivery due to potential harm to the unborn baby. Breastfeeding is not recommended for infants with certain conditions (e.g., jaundice, G6PD deficiency). Drug interactions may alter the effectiveness of medications or increase the risk of side effects. Keep a list of all products used and share it with your healthcare provider. In case of overdose, seek immediate medical attention. Store the medication at room temperature, away from light and moisture, and properly discard it when expired or no longer needed. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
